phonemes.desc: Kappa with a short iota under the acute — the pitch springs high, then the rolled rho snaps it shut, like a falcon turning on the wind.
A second kappa released into the long open eta [ɛː] — the name ends wide and held, never the English 'see'.

pronunciation.approximation: 'KEER-keh' — high pitch on the first syllable, a trilled rho, and a long open final vowel; English 'SUR-see' has wandered far from the falcon's name.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: κίρκος (kírkos), 'hawk, falcon' — also 'ring, circle'; the word her name is usually traced to

kin.label: Latin
kin.form: Circē — whence English 'Circe' and the adjective 'Circean', kept intact through the whole Roman tradition

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: no secure Indo-European etymology; Beekes treats Κίρκη as Pre-Greek, a divine name of the Aegean substrate

pronunciation.note: Kírkē is the boundary case of the Greek list. The Greek Κίρκη carries both features the mechanical tier rule watches for — the acute pitch of the first syllable and the long final eta — and the restoration Kírkē preserves both against the Latinized 'Circe,' which shed them. This entry follows the catalog's Tier-2 assignment; a strict reading of the rule would promote her to the first rank, and her double signature is recorded here so the classification never hardens into doctrine.

domains.title: The Dread Goddess of Aiaia
domains.subtitle: Sorcery, Transformation, and Isolation
domains.lead: Kírkē is the daughter of Hēlios and Perse, sister of Aiētēs, aunt of Médeia — the Sun's child keeping house alone on Aiaia at the edge of the charted world. Homer calls her a dread goddess endowed with speech (δεινὴ θεὸς αὐδήεσσα), polýpharmakos, mistress of many drugs. Her wand does not kill men: it unmakes them, penning the human mind inside the bodies of beasts.

cards.name: Pharmaka
cards.desc: Her art runs through drugs: barley, cheese, and pale honey stirred into Pramneian wine, the pharmaka hidden in the food (Odyssey 10.234–235).

cards.name: Metamorphosis
cards.desc: She is the Greeks' first great thought-experiment on form: the body unmade, the mind left watching from inside the beast.

cards.name: Aiaia
cards.desc: Her island at the world's edge: Homer moors it where the dawn rises; Rome moved it west to the cape that still bears her name.

cards.name: The Great Oath
cards.desc: Beaten at her own art by the moly, she swears the great oath by heaven and earth to plot no further harm against the hero — and keeps it (Odyssey 10.343–346).

symbols.name: The wand (rhábdos)
symbols.meaning: With a single stroke she pens the crew in the sties — the original witch's wand of European literature (Odyssey 10.238)

symbols.name: The cup
symbols.meaning: Barley, cheese, and pale honey in Pramneian wine, with the pharmaka stirred into the food (Odyssey 10.234–235)

symbols.name: Swine
symbols.meaning: Her transformed company: beast in head, voice, bristle, and shape — 'but the mind remained as before' (Odyssey 10.239–243)

symbols.name: The loom
symbols.meaning: The sailors first hear her singing at a great immortal web — goddesses' work, delicate and glorious (Odyssey 10.221–223)

symbols.name: Moly
symbols.meaning: The black-rooted, milk-white-flowered herb Hermes gives against her drugs — hard for mortals to dig (Odyssey 10.302–306)

symbols.name: The falcon
symbols.meaning: Kírkos, the hawk: the word her name is usually traced to — the predator hidden inside the enchantress

mythology.lead: Kírkē's myths turn on the unstable border between human and animal — and on Homer's strangest reversal: the goddess who defeats every man she meets becomes, the hour she is beaten, the hero's most useful ally. The four myths below run from the Odyssey's island to Ovid's Italy, where the enchantress curdles into something darker.

myths.title: The Men Made Swine
myths.text: In Odyssey 10 (208–243), Eurylochus leads twenty-two scouts to Kírkē's hall, past mountain wolves and lions that fawn like dogs — creatures she herself had charmed with evil drugs. She mixes the men a potion of barley, cheese, and pale honey in Pramneian wine, hides pharmaka in the food, strikes them with her wand, and pens them in the sties. They take the heads, the voice, the bristles, and the shape of swine — 'but their mind remained as firm as before' (10.240). Homer does not say she made them beasts; he says the men went on thinking inside the beast, the most quietly horrifying line in the poem. Odysseus comes for them armed with the moly Hermes gives him (10.275–306) — the black-rooted, milk-flowered herb that is hard for mortals to dig, but the gods can do all things. The rescue that follows proves the antidote was never the herb alone: it was the god's counsel, the oath he demands, and the nerve to sit down to a witch's supper. Homer's first monster is a hostess, and his first victory is a well-negotiated dinner.

myths.title: A Year of Feasting, Then the Road to the Dead
myths.text: Her drugs fail against the moly, and Kírkē — recognizing an old prophecy fulfilled — changes sides: she swears the great oath to plot no further harm and takes him to her bed (Odyssey 10.343–346). She restores the crew younger, taller, and fairer than before (10.388–396), and they sit a whole year feasting on abundant flesh and sweet wine (10.467–477). When Odysseus asks to leave, she does not hinder him; she gives him the voyage no living man has sailed — down to the house of Hades and dread Persephone, to consult the soul of the blind seer Teiresias (10.487–540). She names the rock where Pyriphlegethon and Cocytus fall into Acheron and prescribes the blood of a black ram and a ewe to summon the dead. The enchantress becomes the guide: the katabasis of the Odyssey is her itinerary. The poem's geography of the afterlife is drawn not by a prophet or a priest but by a witch with a loom — a quiet assertion that dangerous women hold the maps men lack.

myths.title: Telegonus, the Son Born from Afar
myths.text: Hesiod already knows children of the union: Kírkē, 'in love with steadfast Odysseus,' bears Agrius, Latinus, and Telegonus, 'who ruled over all the much-famed Tyrrhenians' (Theogony 1011–1016 — lines some editors bracket as post-Hesiodic, but our oldest witness to her Italian afterlife). The lost Telegony of Eugammon of Cyrene, preserved in Proclus's summary, completes the tragedy: grown Telegonus sails to find his father and, raiding a coast he does not know, kills Odysseus in ignorance with a spear tipped with a sting-ray's barb — the gentle death 'from the sea' that Teiresias foretold (Odyssey 11.134). He carries the body and Penelope home to Aiaia; Telegonus marries Penelope, Telemachus marries Kírkē herself, and the goddess makes them all immortal and sends them to the Isles of the Blest. The tradition could not bear a simple ending: the man who outwitted every monster is killed by his own unrecognizing son. It is the Trojan cycle's last irony — the hero of recognition dying of a failed one.

myths.title: The Poisoning of Scylla
myths.text: Ovid gives her the witch's cruelest afterlife. The sea-god Glaucus comes to Kírkē for a charm to win the nymph Scylla; Kírkē offers herself instead, is refused, and answers like the daughter of the Sun she is — she grinds her herbs, crosses to the pool, and poisons the water where Scylla bathes (Metamorphoses 14.1–74). Scylla rises to the waist in a ring of barking dogs and becomes the monster of the strait that will one day face Charybdis — the very Scylla whom Kírkē herself teaches Odysseus to pass (Odyssey 12.116–126). In the same book she turns the Latian king Picus into a woodpecker for loving Canens (14.320–434). Rome's Circe does not retire; she curdles the seas and forests of Italy. Where Homer's Kírkē reforms after one defeat, Ovid's knows no such check: power without a guest at the door reverts to type.

lore.syncretism: Rome did not need to invent a Latin Kírkē; it simply moved her in. Hesiod had already posted her sons to the Tyrrhenian coast, and Virgil's Aeneas skirts 'the shores of Circe's land,' where the daughter of the Sun sings ceaselessly in her groves while the groans of her transformed men roll out across the water (Aeneid 7.10–24). The promontory of Circeii claimed her temple (Strabo 5.3.6), and Horace calls Tusculum 'the hills of Telegonus the parricide' (Odes 3.29.8) — her son naturalized as a founder of Latin towns. From there she passes into the European imagination as the archetype of the enchantress: the witch with a pedigree, a loom, and a cup.
lore.culturalLegacy: English keeps her as an adjective: Circean — bewitching, dangerously seductive, charming in the way that unmakes a man. Cape Circeo still bears her name on the Tyrrhenian coast, and if the old derivation of her name from kírkos ('ring; hawk') holds, she shares a root with Latin circus — and so with English circle and circus. The nineteenth century painted her endlessly — Waterhouse's Circe Offering the Cup to Ulysses (1891) and Circe Invidiosa (1892) are the icons — and every island sorceress with a wand and a potion since is her descendant. Restoring Kírkē restores the falcon in the enchantress's name.
lore.extendedMeditation:
The Greeks never decided whether Kírkē was danger or salvation, and Homer refuses to help. He calls her a dread goddess, then lets her feed the hero for a year, arm him against the Sirens and Scylla, and draw him the only map of the underworld Greek epic possesses. She is the poem's most accomplished divinity after Athēnâ — and the only one whose power is chemical. Pharmaka, not thunderbolts: the Greeks suspected that transformation, like poisons and potions, was women's work, and Kírkē is that suspicion deified and stranded on an island where no husband can check her.

Her deepest moment is a piece of grammar: the swine keep their noos, their mind, 'firm as before' (Odyssey 10.240) — what is a person, Homer asks, if the body can be unmade around it? Even her geography is a riddle: he moors Aiaia 'where are the dancing-floors of Dawn and the risings of the sun' (Odyssey 12.3–4), the far east, while Rome dragged her west to the Tyrrhenian cape. The honest answer is that Aiaia lies wherever the charted world ends — and Kírkē is what waits there: the intelligence of the wild, articulate, patient, and not to be trifled with.
lore.archaeology: No excavated sanctuary of Kírkē herself survives; her cult was Roman and coastal. Strabo (5.3.6) reports that the promontory of Circeii — modern Monte Circeo in Lazio — was believed to have once been an island, as Homer's Aiaia was, and that a temple of Circe was pointed out there; the marshy plain behind the cape still shows how the 'island' silted into the mainland. Archaic art took her up earlier than almost any other Homeric episode: Boeotian black-figure vases of the sixth century BCE paint Odysseus drawing his sword on her amid men already bristling into beasts, and an archaic painter is named 'the Circe Painter' for the scene.
